facts.fact_text: The first applicant is a Georgian non-governmental organisation set up to promote and protect the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) people in Georgia.
The first applicant planned to organise a peaceful march on 17 May 2012 in the centre of Tbilisi.
The peaceful march planned by the first applicant was intended to mark the International Day Against Homophobia.
The counter-demonstrators blocked the LGBT marchers' way on Rustaveli Avenue by making a human chain and encircling the marchers, making it impossible for them to pass.
The LGBT marchers were subjected to threats of physical assault and to insults by the counter-demonstrators on Rustaveli Avenue on 17 May 2012.
After approximately twenty to thirty minutes of escalating aggression on 17 May 2012, counter-demonstrators grabbed banners from the hands of several LGBT activists and tore them apart.
Counter-demonstrators resorted to physical attack by pushing and punching the LGBT marchers in the front row on 17 May 2012.
As a result of the counter-demonstrators' assault on 17 May 2012, the sixth applicant (Mr G. Demetrashvili), who was in the front line of the march, was knocked down, beaten and kicked.
The police responded to the third applicant (Mr L. Berianidze) by forcing him into a patrol car on 17 May 2012.

The sixth applicant (Mr G. Demetrashvili), the seventh applicant (Ms G. Dzerkorashvili) and the tenth applicant (Ms M. Kalandadze), all employees of Identoba, were arrested by the police on 17 May 2012 when they moved from the pavement to the road.
On 8 May 2012, the first applicant gave the Tbilisi City Hall prior notice of its intention to hold a peaceful demonstration on 17 May 2012.
On 8 May 2012, the first applicant gave the Ministry of the Interior prior notice of its intention to hold a peaceful demonstration on 17 May 2012.
On 14 May 2012, the Tbilisi City Hall explained to the first applicant the rights and responsibilities of demonstrators as provided for by the relevant law.

In light of a foreseeable protest from those opposed to the LGBT community in Georgia and the general background of hostility towards sexual minorities, the first applicant specifically requested that the authorities provide sufficient protection from possible violence.

The senior officer of the Ministry of the Interior confirmed to the first applicant organisation that police forces would be deployed to ensure that the procession of 17 May 2012 took place peacefully.

In light of a foreseeable protest from those opposed to the LGBT community in Georgia and the general background of hostility towards sexual minorities, the first applicant specifically requested that the authorities provide sufficient protection from possible violence.
The LGBT marchers, feeling threatened on 17 May 2012, immediately telephoned the police to alert them to the danger and request the immediate dispatch of additional police forces.
While waiting for additional police support on 17 May 2012, the LGBT marchers noticed a few police officers present at the scene on Rustaveli Avenue.

When the LGBT marchers approached the police officers present at the scene on 17 May 2012 and asked for help, the officers replied that they were not part of the police patrol and it was not their duty to intervene.
Shortly after the assault on the sixth applicant (Mr G. Demetrashvili), several police patrol cars arrived at the scene on 17 May 2012.
At the time police officers separated the parties on 17 May 2012, the aggressive and agitated counter-demonstrators were still making particularly vitriolic threats against the marchers.
The third applicant (Mr L. Berianidze), who was standing on the pavement with other LGBT marchers on 17 May 2012, asked the police to take more active measures to protect the demonstration.
The police responded to the third applicant (Mr L. Berianidze) by forcing him into a patrol car on 17 May 2012.

As subsequently explained by the Government, the police had sought to distance the third applicant (Mr L. Berianidze) from the scene on 17 May 2012 in order to protect him from the angry counter-demonstrators.

The sixth applicant (Mr G. Demetrashvili), the seventh applicant (Ms G. Dzerkorashvili) and the tenth applicant (Ms M. Kalandadze), all employees of Identoba, were arrested by the police on 17 May 2012 when they moved from the pavement to the road.

The sixth, seventh and tenth applicants (Mr G. Demetrashvili, Ms G. Dzerkorashvili and Ms M. Kalandadze) were forced into police patrol cars and driven around the city for approximately twenty minutes before being returned to Rustaveli Avenue on 17 May 2012.

As subsequently explained by the Government, the aim of the short-term retention of the sixth, seventh and tenth applicants on 17 May 2012 was to prevent them from committing an administrative offence of impeding road traffic.

As subsequently explained by the Government, the aim of the short-term retention of the sixth, seventh and tenth applicants on 17 May 2012 was also to protect them from the counter-demonstrators' assault.

On 18 May 2012, members of the board of the first applicant organisation filed several complaints with the Ministry of the Interior concerning the violent acts committed during the march of 17 May 2012 by representatives of the Orthodox Parents' Union and the Saint King Vakhtang Gorgasali's Brotherhood.

On 18 May 2012, members of the board of the first applicant organisation filed several complaints with the Chief Public Prosecutor's Office concerning the violent acts committed during the march of 17 May 2012 by representatives of the Orthodox Parents' Union and the Saint King Vakhtang Gorgasali's Brotherhood.

On 26 June 2012, the first applicant received a letter from the deputy director of the police patrol department of the Ministry of the Interior in response to the board members' complaints of 18 May 2012.

The letter of 26 June 2012 from the deputy director of the police patrol department of the Ministry of the Interior stated that there were no signs of illegality in the actions of the police during the demonstration of 17 May 2012.

The letter of 26 June 2012 from the deputy director of the police patrol department of the Ministry of the Interior stated that there was no need to launch an investigation against the police for abuse of power.
Two counter-demonstrators had been arrested for transgression under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences (minor breach of public order) in connection with the events of 17 May 2012.

The two counter-demonstrators arrested for minor breach of public order under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences were each fined 100 Georgian laris (approximately 45 euros) in connection with the events of 17 May 2012.

In their criminal complaints of 3 and 5 July 2012, the applicants specifically requested that a criminal investigation be launched on account of the verbal and physical attacks perpetrated against them by the counter-demonstrators with clear discriminatory intent.

In their criminal complaints of 3 and 5 July 2012, the applicants specifically requested that a criminal investigation be launched on account of the acts and/or omissions of the police officers who had failed to protect them from the assaults on 17 May 2012.

In their criminal complaints of 3 and 5 July 2012, the applicants emphasised that criminal inquiries should be conducted with due regard to Article 53 of the Criminal Code of Georgia, which provided that the existence of homophobic intent was an aggravating circumstance in the commission of a criminal offence.

By a letter of 17 July 2012, the Ministry of the Interior replied to the first applicant and the second to fourteenth applicants that during the incident of 17 May 2012 the police had called upon both the LGBT marchers and the counter-demonstrators to exercise their right to demonstrate in a peaceful manner.

The Ministry of the Interior's letter of 17 July 2012 reiterated the information concerning the imposition of administrative sanctions on two of the counter-demonstrators, namely their arrest and fine of 100 Georgian laris each under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
On 24 October 2012, a criminal investigation was opened into the alleged beating of the sixth applicant (Mr G. Demetrashvili) by unidentified persons on 17 May 2012.

According to the latest information available in the case file, the criminal investigation opened on 19 May 2012 into the light bodily injuries sustained by the fourteenth applicant (Ms M. Tsutskiridze) is still pending.

According to the latest information available in the case file, the criminal investigation opened on 24 October 2012 into the light bodily injuries sustained by the sixth applicant (Mr G. Demetrashvili) is still pending.
The sixth applicant (Mr G. Demetrashvili) has never been granted victim status in the criminal investigation into his injuries.
The fourteenth applicant (Ms M. Tsutskiridze) has never been granted victim status in the criminal investigation into her injuries.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 was adopted by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe on 31 March 2010 on measures to combat discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that member states should ensure effective, prompt and impartial investigations into alleged cases of crimes and other incidents where the sexual orientation or gender identity of the victim is reasonably suspected to have constituted a motive for the perpetrator.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that member states should ensure that particular attention is paid to the investigation of crimes and incidents allegedly committed by law enforcement officials or by other persons acting in an official capacity, and that those responsible are effectively brought to justice and, where appropriate, punished in order to avoid impunity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that member states should ensure that law enforcement authorities take appropriate measures to protect participants in peaceful demonstrations in favour of the human rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons from any attempts to unlawfully disrupt or inhibit the effective enjoyment of their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
The study on Discrimination on Grounds of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity in Europe found that in Georgia 84% of respondents expressed negative attitudes towards homosexuality.

In 2010, before a debate in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe on a report focusing on LGBT human rights, different religious communities in Georgia collaboratively protested about 'abnormalities, such as homosexuality, bisexuality and other sexual perversions'.

The Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 12 September 2014 noted that NGOs had expressed serious concerns regarding the lack of effective investigation and adequate punishment for perpetrators of attacks against LGBTI persons in Georgia.

The Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 12 September 2014 encouraged increased efforts to enhance tolerance and non-discrimination among the majority population in Georgia, and emphasised the importance for authorities, public actors and community leaders to send an unambiguous message in favour of human rights and tolerance, and against violence, hate speech and discrimination.

The International Lesbian and Gay Association (ILGA) noted in its 2013 Annual Review that the government of Georgia did not take measures to ensure effective implementation of the amended Article 53 of the Criminal Code, such as training the relevant police officers or taking actions to build confidence between law enforcement forces and the LGBT community.
